pedagogy.summary: At ages 6–7 this is about noticing and describing PREDICTABLE patterns from direct observation — the Sun appears to rise on one side, cross the sky and set on the other each day; the Moon changes shape over about a month; and stars appear at night but not in the day. It is taught through sustained first-hand observation and simple recording (a month-long Moon-shape diary, marking where the Sun is at different times), keeping firmly to describing and predicting the patterns rather than explaining their causes, which are deferred to later topics.
bestPractices: Ground the topic in first-hand and media observation over time — a month-long Moon-shape diary, marking the Sun's position morning/midday/afternoon, noticing stars only at night.
Focus on describing and PREDICTING the pattern (what will the Moon look like next week?), matching the crosscutting concept that patterns can be observed and used to predict.
Keep strictly to observation, not mechanism — do not yet explain why the Moon's shape changes or why the Sun appears to move; premature causes confuse at this age.
Use consistent recording formats (shape drawings, photos, a class calendar) so the pattern emerges from the child's own data.
Note carefully that the Sun and Moon APPEAR to move/change — record what is seen without over-claiming the cause.
Gently correct 'stars aren't there in the daytime' — they are, but the Sun outshines them — while keeping the lesson observational.
keyRepresentations: A Moon-phase diary strip — the shape drawn each night across about a month.
A daytime Sun-path arc with morning/midday/afternoon positions marked.
A day-sky vs night-sky sort (Sun by day; stars by night; the Moon sometimes in both).
A calendar/timeline showing the pattern repeating.
commonMisconceptions: The Moon changes shape because clouds or something covers part of it, or it is a different Moon each night.
The Moon only appears at night — in fact it is often visible during the day.
Stars are not present in the daytime — they are there but outshone by the Sun.
The patterns of Sun, Moon and stars are random rather than predictable.
The Sun literally travels across the sky (recording the appearance is fine; the correct cause is deferred).

learn.summary: For ages 6–7, learners notice, describe and PREDICT repeating sky patterns from sustained first-hand observation: the Sun appears to rise on one side, arc across the sky and set on the other each day; the Moon changes shape over about a month; and stars are seen at night (but are still present, outshone, by day). Teaching stays firmly at describing and predicting patterns, deferring their causes to later topics. Core activities are a month-long Moon-shape diary, safely marking the Sun's position at morning/midday/afternoon by reading a shadow stick (never looking at the Sun), and a day-sky vs night-sky sort. A screen 'sky over time' scrubber and static phase/Sun-arc references are useful supports, and a short sequence/sort check can assess the pattern knowledge.

activities.title: Month-long Moon-shape diary
feedback: If a learner says it is 'a different Moon each night' or that clouds cover part of it, point back to the ordered diary strip: it is the same Moon, and the shape changes gradually and repeats. Clouds can hide part of the Moon on some nights, but the slowly changing shape seen on clear nights is not made by clouds.
If a learner is surprised to see the Moon in daytime, affirm the real sighting — the Moon rises and sets at different times, so it is sometimes up in daylight.
Praise predictions that use the recorded pattern (e.g. 'it has been getting fatter, so next it will be fatter still, until it is full and then starts getting thinner') rather than guesses.
activities.rationale: The objective is a conceptual pattern over time, so first-hand recording over about a month lets the pattern emerge from the child's own data, and the predict-then-check step targets the crosscutting idea that observed patterns can be used to predict. Mechanism (why the shape changes) is deliberately deferred at this age.

learnerActions: Whenever the Moon can be seen in a clear sky (often in the evening, but on some nights it is not up at a child's evening viewing time or cannot be seen at all), draw the shape of the Moon you can see, dating each drawing, and mark 'not seen' on other nights.
Keep the drawings in order on a strip or class calendar so the sequence builds up over about a month.
After a week or two, look back at the pattern and PREDICT: draw what you think the Moon will look like in a few nights.
Check your prediction against the next real observation and talk about whether the shape is fattening or thinning.
Watch for and record any time you spot the Moon in the daytime too.
activities.intendedInsight: The Moon's shape changes in a dependable, repeating cycle over about a month, so you can use past observations to predict what comes next — and the Moon is sometimes visible by day, not only at night.

activities.title: Mark the Sun's daily path
feedback: Always record that the Sun APPEARS to move/rise/set — accept and praise the observed pattern without yet claiming the Sun itself travels; the cause (Earth's rotation) comes later.
Reinforce safe observation: positions are read from the shadow stick's shadow, never by looking at the Sun.
If a learner puts stars only in 'night', accept it for the sort but add that the stars are still there in the day, just hidden by the bright sky.
Reinforce correct predictions by linking them to the earlier observations the learner made.
activities.rationale: Marking real positions at set times and predicting the next position keeps the focus on describing and predicting an observable pattern. Reading the Sun's position indirectly from a shadow (never looking at the Sun) protects young children's eyes, and wording it as 'appears to move' avoids cementing a cause that the topic defers.
sourceClaims: NGSS 1-ESS1-1: '[curriculum wording omitted; reference 1-ESS1-1]' — examples include the sun and moon appearing to rise, [curriculum wording omitted; reference 1-ESS1-1] being [curriculum wording omitted; reference 1-ESS1-1]; [curriculum wording omitted; reference 1-ESS1-1].
learnerActions: At morning, midday and afternoon on the same day, record where the Sun appears — safely and indirectly, by marking the shadow cast by a fixed stick or object (a shadow stick); the Sun is on the opposite side of the stick from its shadow. NEVER look at or stare directly at the Sun.

Compare the three recorded positions and describe the path: the Sun appears to climb higher towards midday (shortest shadow) and then get lower in the afternoon, fitting the pattern of rising on one side and setting on the other.
Predict where the Sun will appear at lunchtime (or another time), then check by reading the shadow again — not by looking at the Sun.
Sort a set of sky objects/pictures into 'seen by day', 'seen by night', and 'sometimes both' (Sun by day; stars by night; Moon sometimes in both).
activities.intendedInsight: The Sun follows the same daily rising-arcing-setting pattern (only shifting slowly over the seasons), so its apparent position at a given time is predictable; the Sun is seen by day and the stars by night, while the Moon can be seen in either.

activities.title: Dim-light predict-observe-explain (stars hidden by day)
feedback: The diagnostic is the pre-observation reason: a child who predicts 'it goes off' may be holding the stars-disappear idea — check by asking about the stars directly.

If a learner explains daytime invisibility by the stars being absent, respond: the stars are still there; the daytime sky is simply too bright to see them — like a small dim light that is hard to see in a brightly-lit room.
Target answer to voice and reinforce: 'You can't see the stars in the daytime because the sky is too bright — the Sun's light washes them out — but the stars are still there all along.'
activities.rationale: This is a predict-observe-explain analogy chosen to surface and address the common misconception that stars are physically absent by day. The pre-observation reason, followed by a direct question about the stars, can help tell a child who thinks stars vanish from one who thinks the bright sky hides them.
sourceClaims: A common misconception is that stars are not present during the day and that the Moon appears only at night; children also treat the Sun's apparent motion as real — documented children's ideas about familiar astronomical events.
learnerActions: In a darkened room, turn on a small dim LED night-light.
Before anything changes, PREDICT with a reason: when all the big room lights come on, will the little light still be shining or will it go off? Commit to your answer out loud.
Turn on all the big lights and watch — the little light becomes much harder to see and may seem to vanish, even though it is still on.
Dim the room again and watch it reappear.
Say what this shows about why we can't see the stars in the daytime.
activities.intendedInsight: A dim light is still on even when a much brighter light washes it out — just as the stars are still present in the daytime but hidden by the bright, Sun-lit sky.

activities.title: Scrubbable 'sky over time' model (optional support)
feedback: When a prediction is checked and matches, name the takeaway: the pattern is predictable and repeats.
If a static phase strip or Sun-arc picture is used instead, note it is a reference only — it cannot be advanced in time, so pair it with the real-sky diary and predict-then-check talk.
Keep using the learner's own diary alongside the model so the represented pattern and the observed pattern stay connected.
activities.rationale: A time-scrubbable model can make the pattern-over-time and predict-then-check idea concrete; a single static image cannot be advanced in time, so it serves only as a reference. The diary capture ties the model back to first-hand observation. A 3D sky dome is not needed here, since the observable pattern reads clearly in 2D and the mechanism that might motivate 3D is deferred. This is a proposed support, not a validated intervention or a replacement for real observation.

learnerActions: Drag a time slider forward: watch the Sun rise from one horizon, arc across the sky and set as the world darkens and stars appear.
Keep dragging across weeks and watch the Moon steadily fatten and thin through its shapes.
Before checking, predict: what will tonight's Moon look like, or where will the Sun be at lunchtime? Then drag to check.
Use a built-in Moon-diary capture that mirrors the shapes you have been recording in the real sky.
activities.intendedInsight: The sky's changes are a dependable, repeating pattern — not random — so advancing time lets you anticipate the next state, and the on-screen cycle lines up with your own real observations.

activities.title: Pattern check: sequence and sort
feedback: Full understanding: describes the patterns AND explains stars are still present by day but hidden by the bright sky, and knows the Moon cycles over about a month and is sometimes visible by day.
Partial: describes the patterns but explains star-invisibility by 'they're not there' rather than 'the sky is too bright' — reteach with the dim-light demo.
Gap: thinks stars and Moon appear and disappear with no sense of a repeating pattern — return to the diary and Sun-path observations.
activities.rationale: Sequencing, next-shape choice, and the two-tier star question let you assess the pattern knowledge, and the reason tier is essential because both the correct and the misconception learner answer 'no' to simply 'can you see stars by day?'. Recognition/sequencing tasks can check pattern knowledge but do not by themselves elicit the sustained first-hand recording the topic is grounded in.
sourceClaims: A common misconception is that stars are not present during the day and that the Moon appears only at night; children also treat the Sun's apparent motion as real — documented children's ideas about familiar astronomical events.
learnerActions: Put a scrambled set of Moon-phase pictures back into the correct order.
Given the last few Moon shapes in order, choose which shape comes next.
Sort sky objects into day-sky vs night-sky (with 'sometimes both' available for the Moon).
Answer and give a reason: in the daytime, can you see the stars? Why do you think that is?
activities.intendedInsight: Demonstrate that you can describe and predict the sky patterns and explain that daytime stars are hidden, not gone.

constraints: Keep strictly to describing and predicting observable patterns; do NOT yet explain why the Moon's shape changes or why the Sun appears to move — premature causes confuse at this age and are deferred to later topics.
Always record that the Sun and Moon APPEAR to move/change; do not cement 'the Sun moves' or 'the Sun travels across the sky' as the cause.
Observe the Sun safely: children must never look directly at or stare at the Sun. Record its apparent position only indirectly, using shadows (e.g. a shadow stick).

Ground the topic in sustained first-hand observation over time (about a month for the Moon); screen models and static phase/Sun-arc pictures are supports, not substitutes for the child's own sky data.
A static phase strip or Sun-arc picture is a useful reference but cannot be advanced in time; pair it with predict-then-check against real observation.
Recognition/sequencing/sorting tasks can assess pattern knowledge but do not elicit the independent, sustained recording the objective requires.
Gently correct 'stars aren't there in the daytime' (they are, but outshone) and 'the Moon only comes out at night' (it is often visible by day) while keeping the lesson observational.
Moon diary and Sun-path recording depend on clear weather and the Moon being up — plan for nights the sky is not observable.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
One cited source (IOPSpark children's-ideas claim) is marked verified:false in the row; the NGSS 1-ESS1-1 claim is marked verified:true. Treat the misconception citations accordingly.

The original framed a 3D sky dome as 'unnecessary' and a static image as unable to deliver the 'crosscutting payoff'. These comparative/necessity claims are not established by the sources; softened to narrowly scoped affordances (static images are references that cannot be advanced in time; 2D reads the pattern well; 3D is not needed here).

The original rated dialogue/conversation 'poor' partly on persona and early-reader grounds; this was not propagated as a universal law — spoken prediction and reasoning are retained inside the predict-observe-explain and two-tier tasks.

The original row contained no eye-safety guidance for locating the Sun; a safe-observation instruction (read the Sun's position indirectly from a shadow stick, never look at or stare at the Sun) has been added to the Sun-path activity and constraints as a correction, not an original field. An earlier draft that allowed 'brief glances' at the Sun was removed as unsafe for this age.
Self-review found no arithmetic or force/motion errors to correct. The 'Sun appears to move' phrasing is preserved as an idealisation consistent with deferring the rotation cause at this age.

assess.poeTask: In a bright room, switch on a small dim LED night-light and ask the child to PREDICT with a reason: when I turn on all the big room lights, will the little light still be shining, or will it go off? Have them commit. Turn the big lights on — the LED seems to vanish. Then dim the room and it reappears. The child sees the little light was on the whole time, just washed out — mirroring how the stars are still there in the daytime, hidden by the bright sky. The pre-observation reason is the diagnostic part: a child who predicts 'it goes off' is holding the stars-disappear idea.
probeDeeper: If the stars are still there in the daytime, why can't we see them?
The Moon looked full last night — will it look exactly the same tomorrow, or does its shape change? Over how long?
Sometimes you can see the Moon in the afternoon. Does that surprise you? What does it tell us?
assess.correctAnswer: You can't see the stars in the daytime because the sky is too bright — the Sun's light washes them out — but the stars are still there all along.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'you can't see stars in the day because they're not there — they come out at night' (stars physically appear and disappear)
errorPatterns.nextMove: The stars stay put; the daytime sky is simply too bright to see them — like a small torch you can't see across a brightly-lit room.
errorPatterns.distractor: Because the stars are not in the sky in the daytime.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: explains daytime invisibility by the stars being absent rather than hidden

errorPatterns.pattern: 'the Moon only comes out at night — it isn't there in the day' (Moon is a night-only object)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Point out real daytime-Moon sightings; the Moon rises and sets at different times, so it is sometimes up in daylight.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: is surprised the Moon can be seen in daytime; says the Moon belongs to the night

errorPatterns.pattern: 'the Sun travels across the sky on its own' (apparent-motion read as the Sun moving)
errorPatterns.nextMove: At this age accept the observed rising/setting pattern but do not cement 'the Sun moves' as the cause — that explanation is built later with Earth's rotation.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: describes the Sun as journeying across the sky by itself

responseLevels.gap: Thinks stars and the Moon appear and disappear (not there in the day); no sense of a repeating, predictable pattern.
responseLevels.full: Describes the predictable sky patterns and explains that stars are still present in the day but hidden by the bright sky; knows the Moon's shape cycles over about a month and that the Moon is sometimes visible in daytime.
responseLevels.partial: Describes the patterns (Sun up in the day, stars at night, Moon changing shape) but explains star-invisibility by 'they're not there' rather than 'the sky is too bright.'

assess.diagnosticPrompt: In the daytime, can you see the stars in the sky? … Now tell me why you think that is.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Both a child who thinks the stars vanish in daytime and one who thinks the bright sky hides them answer 'no' to the first tier — the reason tier is what separates them. A child reasoning correctly says the stars are still there but hidden by the bright sky; the misconception child says the stars go away, come out at night, or aren't there in the day.
